featured.title: The Singleton design pattern enables parallel execution????
featured.summary:
A simple way to think about it
A Singleton is like one shared printer in an office. Many people can send print jobs at the same time, but if the printer doesn’t handle jobs properly, documents can get mixed up. The pattern gives you one shared object; thread safety is what makes parallel use safe.
featured.author: Abhishek Chowdhury
featured.body:
Not really. The Singleton pattern doesn’t “allow parallel execution” by itself—it just makes sure there’s only one instance of a class, shared by everyone who needs it.

What that means in practice
Several threads can call methods on that one shared object at the same time, so in that sense it can be used in a parallel environment. But whether that’s safe depends entirely on how the Singleton is written.

If the Singleton has no changing state, multiple threads can usually use it safely.

If it has mutable fields, threads can overwrite each other’s data, causing race conditions or unexpected behavior.

If the Singleton is created lazily without proper synchronization, two threads might both see it as null and accidentally create two instances—breaking the whole point of the pattern.

When you need separate instances
Sometimes one shared object is actually the wrong choice. For example, in parallel test automation, each thread often needs its own browser session. In that case, developers use ThreadLocal so every thread gets its own instance, rather than forcing everyone to share one.

So the short version: Singleton gives you one shared object; parallel execution works only if that object is thread-safe.

articles.title: Fallback mechanism is required for element identifier in automation framework???
articles.summary: Applications change frequently, so locators can break after small UI updates. Fallback locators let the framework try another safe way to find an element. Use a stable, meaningful primary locator—such as a unique ID or accessibility attribute—and reserve fallbacks for cases where they’re needed. Log whenever a fallback is used.
articles.author: Abhishek Chowdhury
articles.body:
Yes, a fallback mechanism for identifying UI elements is highly recommended in an automation framework—but it should be treated as a backup, not a replacement for stable locators.

Why it is important
UI elements can change because of:

Dynamic IDs or class names.

Minor UI redesigns.

Changes in DOM structure.

Different environments or browsers.

Responsive layouts.

If the framework depends on only one locator, even a small UI change can fail the test. A fallback strategy allows the framework to try another reliable way to identify the same element instead of failing immediately. This approach is commonly used in self-healing automation.

Example
Suppose you need to click a Login button. The framework could try:

Stable element ID.

Accessibility label or role.

A reliable CSS selector.

Text-based identification.

XPath as a last structured option.

Image recognition or OCR only as a final fallback.

A typical sequence would be:

text
Try ID
  ↓ if not found
Try accessibility role
  ↓ if not found
Try CSS selector
  ↓ if not found
Try text or XPath
  ↓ if still not found
Log the failure and stop safely
Important caution
Fallback should not silently click any element that looks similar. Before interacting, the framework should verify that the element is:

Visible.

Enabled.

Unique.

The correct type, such as a button or input.

Located in the expected page or container.

If confidence is low, it is safer to fail with a clear error than to interact with the wrong element. Some automation platforms use validation and confidence checks for exactly this reason.
